analysis.one_liner: Imposes a binding ethics code, stricter recusal rules, and public complaint procedures on Supreme Court justices.
analysis.headline: The Supreme Court ethics bill was introduced with 35 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make Supreme Court justices follow a written ethics code with public procedures for handling complaints about misconduct. It would tighten the rules on when a justice must step aside from a case — including if a party gave the justice or their family money or gifts, or spent heavily to support their appointment. It would also force lawyers and outside groups who weigh in on cases to disclose gifts or payments to justices, and require public notice whenever a judge is disqualified from a case. The bill has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who appear before the courts. The bill would make it possible for the public to see the ethics rules governing the nine Supreme Court justices, file a complaint when a justice appears conflicted, and learn when and why a judge had to step away from a case. Litigants before the Court would learn whether the people deciding their case received gifts or money from the other side, and outside groups' financial backing of briefs would be disclosed.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue, publish, and make searchable on its website a binding code of conduct for the justices.

Creates a complaint process: anyone can file a sworn complaint alleging a justice violated the ethics code or recusal law, and a randomly selected panel of five chief circuit judges can investigate, hold hearings, issue subpoenas, and recommend discipline, with public reports when a complaint is not dismissed.

Expands the legal duty to step aside: a justice must recuse if a party in the case spent substantial money to help put that justice on the Court, or if a party gave the justice, their spouse, or their minor child a gift, income, or reimbursement within six years of the case.

Lets a party who loses a recusal motion get that decision reviewed — for Supreme Court justices, by the other eight justices; for lower-court judges, by a random panel of three outside judges — with public notice and reasons posted whenever a judge is disqualified.

Requires lawyers and outside groups who weigh in on a case to disclose any gifts, payments, or lobbying they provided to the justices, and requires amicus groups to disclose who funds them, with an annual government audit of compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices and the Court itself as an institution, which would lose its status as the only federal court whose judges answer to no binding ethics code. Wealthy litigants and well-connected interest groups that currently give justices gifts or fund groups supporting the justices would face mandatory disclosure, and parties that spent money to support a justice's appointment could find that justice barred from hearing their cases. Groups filing friend-of-the-court briefs would bear new disclosure and audit costs.

drawbacks.text: Recusal decisions involving lower-court judges would be reviewed by panels of other federal judges, and complaints about Supreme Court justices would still be handled by a panel of sitting chief circuit judges — insiders reviewing insiders, which critics say falls short of independent enforcement.

The complaint process allows sanctions against people who file frivolous or harassing complaints, a provision critics could use to argue it deters legitimate whistleblowers, and the process still depends on the Court's own compliance.
Codes of conduct must be issued by the Supreme Court itself after public comment, so the Court retains significant control over the content of its own ethics rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest: clearer ethical rules, enforceable recusal, and public disclosure of who pays for access to the Court. The main costs are the risk of harassment complaints against judges and heavier administrative burdens; an honest supporter would acknowledge that complaint procedures can be abused and that the bill cannot force a resistant Court to embrace rigorous self-investigation. The main good-faith objection is that subjecting the Supreme Court to outside review of its recusal decisions alters the separation of powers, though the bill tries to blunt this by making the remaining justices the panel for their own colleague.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 20, 2025 and, the same day, was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action is listed: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action has occurred since the referral.
All 35 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chief Justice John Roberts has said the Court polices itself, and the justices now keep the status quo: no enforceable code, no outside complaint process, and recusal decisions that stay entirely their own. Groups that spend on cases before the Court also keep filing without disclosing what they gave the justices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The justices, who face no new rules

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 original Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 35 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a Senate majority of sponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Republican has signed on, so the bill lacks the 60 votes typically needed to advance on the Senate floor.

industries.note: The bill strips away the Court's ability to police its own ethics: justices would face a written code, a complaint process, mandatory recusal for financial ties to parties, and outside review of recusal decisions. It directly targets self-dealing by officeholders.

industries.industry: Litigants, trade associations, and advocacy groups that file Supreme Court briefs (including business and industry-backed amicus groups)
industries.note: Groups that spend heavily on the Court would have to publicly disclose gifts to justices, spending on justices' appointments, and their funding. Heavy Court users face new compliance costs and increased transparency about who is influencing cases.

analysis.trajectory: A bill referred to Senate Judiciary with no hearing or markup on the calendar, and no Republican cosponsors, is unlikely to reach the Senate floor this Congress. Similar Supreme Court ethics bills have stalled in committee in past Congresses; the most realistic path would require Judiciary action and a 60-vote floor threshold the current cosponsor count does not meet.
